item_title: Constellation Energy's chief executive said the market had overreacted to the midterm results out of fear that Democrats will not let data centres get built, The Verge reported (Nov 16)
mechanism: Power, construction and chip stocks were priced on the data-centre buildout continuing, so fear of Democratic limits on siting repriced them together.

scenarios.direction: Democratic proposals on data-centre siting stay narrow, and AI-adjacent stocks win back part of the sell-off.
scenarios.why: Constellation's chief executive said Democrats do not want to be the reason the economy takes a nosedive by halting data-centre development, The Verge reported.

scenarios.direction: State and local limits spread, slowing projects, and builders and power sellers stay at a discount.
scenarios.why: The Verge wrote that the fight has been fragmented and hyperlocal but could change, and noted Republican Virginia lawmakers have also pursued data-centre regulation.
scenarios.precedent: In 2021 Ireland's grid operator EirGrid said it would not connect new Dublin data centres before 2028.

scenarios.direction: Federal action to take siting control from the states advances, and the policy-risk discount on power and construction names narrows.
scenarios.why: The Verge reported the Trump administration is working to wrest some control over data-centre development away from the states.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, has no reading on power or data-centre equities, so this rests on the reporting alone.

item_title: Nvidia's Form 8-K states a maximum gross exposure under guarantees of $118.0 billion at Oct 25, 2026, including $105.0 billion of SB Energy credit support (Nov 17)
mechanism: Nvidia's guarantees put part of its customers' credit risk on its own balance sheet, so a customer's failure to pay could fall on Nvidia as well as on lenders.

scenarios.direction: No guarantee is called, and the exposure stays a disclosure item as the customers pay.
scenarios.why: The 8-K figure is a maximum gross exposure, a ceiling on what could be owed and not an amount owed.

scenarios.direction: Lenders and rating agencies treat the guarantees as debt-like and price Nvidia's credit and its customers' loans accordingly.
scenarios.why: Reuters reported on Oct 1 that lenders wanted more guarantees from Nvidia on its chip-backed financing plan because they doubted GPUs would earn revenue for a decade.

scenarios.direction: A data-centre customer under strain misses payments and Nvidia is called on a guarantee, taking a charge.
scenarios.why: SB Energy, which accounts for $105.0 billion of the exposure, postponed its IPO marketing in September to answer SEC questions, Reuters reported.
scenarios.precedent: Lucent Technologies' financing of telecom customers, including Winstar Communications, which filed for bankruptcy in April 2001, ended in bad-debt charges.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, has no reading on vendor financing or Nvidia's guarantees, so this rests on the reporting alone.

item_title: Crunchbase News reported (Nov 18), from Anthropic's S-1, a purchase and lease agreement for $895.4 billion of compute, of which $447.5 billion will be incurred before the end of 2030
mechanism: A compute commitment fixed in dollars ties Anthropic's IPO cash and revenue growth to payments owed to its chip and cloud suppliers, so those suppliers' order books depend on its finances.

scenarios.direction: Revenue keeps compounding and the IPO cash covers the 2026 to 2030 payments on schedule.
scenarios.why: Crunchbase News reported Q3 2026 revenue of $17 billion, up 12x in a year, and over $100 billion already on Anthropic's balance sheet.

scenarios.direction: Growth slows and Anthropic seeks to defer or resize commitments, pressing suppliers' backlogs and financing.
scenarios.why: The $447.5 billion due by 2030 is a fixed dollar amount, while the revenue that must pay for it is not fixed.
scenarios.precedent: WeWork's 2019 S-1 showed about $47 billion of lease commitments; the IPO was pulled that September and WeWork filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

scenarios.direction: Listed equity becomes a repeatable financing channel for further compute deals, easing reliance on private rounds.
scenarios.why: TechCrunch reported the IPO priced above range, selling 980 million shares for $81.3 billion, so public demand for the stock appeared strong.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, has no reading on AI-lab financing, so this rests on the day's reporting alone.

item_title: TechCrunch reported that Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion to cover its compute commitments over the next 12 months and $451.6 billion before the end of 2030 (Nov 19), and WIRED reported more than $900 billion owed to vendors over 19 years
mechanism: Fixed-dollar compute commitments set against cash raised mean Anthropic's suppliers' order books depend on its revenue path after the IPO funds are spent.

scenarios.direction: Cash of about $200 to $220 billion covers the $70.7 billion due within 12 months with room to spare.
scenarios.why: TechCrunch's and WIRED's cash figures are roughly three times the 12-month commitment TechCrunch reported.

scenarios.direction: Revenue falls short of what the 2030 commitments need, and Anthropic seeks to defer or resize them, pressing suppliers.
scenarios.why: The $451.6 billion due by 2030 exceeds the reported cash by over $230 billion, and SemiAnalysis's estimate of $280 billion in revenue needed over four years is an estimate, not a contract.
scenarios.precedent: WeWork's 2019 S-1 disclosed about $47 billion of lease commitments against 2018 revenue of about $1.8 billion; it filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

scenarios.direction: The share price staying above the $83 IPO price lets Anthropic and its partners raise further equity for compute.
scenarios.why: TechCrunch reported shares trading at $111.50 in early trade, 33% above the IPO price, so public demand appeared strong on day one.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, has no reading on AI-lab financing, so this rests on the day's reporting alone.

item_title: TechCrunch reported (Nov 20), citing Compute Credit Index Research, that some Nvidia H100 chips are selling for about half of their original 2023 cost basis, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024
mechanism: Lenders to data-centre builders lean on chips' resale value as collateral, so a fall in used-chip prices raises borrowing costs or tightens loan terms.

scenarios.direction: Resale prices hold near current levels, and chip-backed loans keep pricing off collateral that retains value.
scenarios.why: TechCrunch reported some H200 configurations selling at their 2024 introduction price, which supports the lenders' resale backstop.

scenarios.direction: A newer chip generation pushes H100 resale prices well below half of cost, and lenders ask for more collateral or higher rates.
scenarios.why: H100s already sell at about half of their 2023 cost basis per the index, so further falls would erode the cushion that makes this debt cheap.
scenarios.precedent: After Ethereum's September 2022 move to proof-of-stake cut demand for mining GPUs, miners such as Core Scientific, which had borrowed against equipment, filed for Chapter 11 in December 2022.

scenarios.direction: Lenders add conditions on where chips may be used, as SpaceX's lenders reportedly asked about orbital sites.
scenarios.why: A chip in orbit cannot be repossessed and resold, so a lender's backstop depends on where the chips sit, which TechCrunch reported lenders tried to restrict.

context_note: The standing capital-context snapshot, last refreshed 2026-08-25, has no reading on chip-backed financing, so this rests on the day's reporting alone.
